names.note: In Argentina 'algarrobo negro' is the standard name; 'algarrobo morado' and 'algarrobo dulce' are regional names, and 'ibopé-hú' is its Guaraní name in the northeast.

range_note: Gran Chaco, Espinal and northern Monte of Argentina (including Córdoba up to 1,500 m in southern sierras), Bolivia, Paraguay, Uruguay and southern Brazil.

summary.en: A native Chaco and Espinal tree with a short, dark furrowed trunk and a wide, rounded umbrella crown of airy bipinnate leaves. In spring it hangs pale-yellow flower spikes, followed in summer by sweet, beaded yellow pods blotched with dark purple.
summary.es: Árbol nativo del Chaco y el Espinal, de tronco corto, oscuro y surcado y copa ancha, redondeada y aparasolada de hojas bipinnadas aireadas. En primavera cuelga espigas florales amarillo pálido y en verano da chauchas dulces y arrosariadas, amarillas con manchas violáceas.

sources.title: Flora del Cono Sur / Flora Argentina: Neltuma nigra (Griseb.) C.E. Hughes & G.P. Lewis var. nigra (Instituto de Botánica Darwinion)
Galera, F. M. (2000). Las especies del género Prosopis (Algarrobos) de América Latina con especial énfasis en aquellas de interés económico — I.2.23 Prosopis nigra. FCA-UNC / FAO, Córdoba.
Sistema de Información de Biodiversidad (SIB), Administración de Parques Nacionales: Neltuma nigra (citing Digilio & Legname 1966)

Gaillard de Benítez, C., Pece, M., Juárez de Galíndez, M. & Acosta, M. (2014). Modelaje de la biomasa aérea individual y otras relaciones dendrométricas de Prosopis nigra Gris. en la provincia de Santiago del Estero, Argentina. Quebracho 22(1): 17-29.
Giménez, A. M. & Moglia, J. G. (2003). Árboles del Chaco Argentino: Guía para el reconocimiento dendrológico (Ficha 45: Prosopis nigra). FCF-UNSE, Santiago del Estero.
INTI-CITEMA: Densidad de maderas argentinas (Prosopis nigra)
CADAMDA: Ficha Técnica Algarrobo Negro (Prosopis nigra)
iNaturalist: Neltuma nigra (taxon 1493150, research-grade observations and phenology histograms)

adult_height_m.note: Galera (2000) gives 4-10 m with occasional trees to 16 m; Flora Argentina up to 15 m; Giménez & Moglia (2003) up to 16 m; SIB (Digilio & Legname 1966) 3-8 m; 30 Dry Chaco trees in Gaillard de Benítez et al. (2014) averaged 9.17 m (range 5.5-12 m).

crown_width_m.note: Geometric mean of major and minor crown diameters across 30 Dry Chaco trees in Santiago del Estero (major 5.32-17.0 m, mean 11.94 m; minor 3.7-15.8 m, mean 10.08 m).

trunk_dbh_m.note: Galera (2000) gives 0.5-0.8 m; Giménez & Moglia (2003) 0.6-1.1 m; SIB up to 0.4 m; 30 Dry Chaco trees in Gaillard de Benítez et al. (2014) ranged 0.12-0.60 m (mean 0.35 m).

height_m.note: Eight-year-old cultivated trees in Córdoba (Galera 1998 in Galera 2000, mean 3.51 ± 0.48 m).

leaf_out.note: In Córdoba bud break starts in early September with peak swelling in mid-September (Galera 2000); bright new foliage shows in October photos r01, r06 and r15.

flowering.note: In Córdoba flower buds appear in late September and peak in late October (Galera 2000); iNaturalist flowering histogram records September (2), October (8) and November (1), with Córdoba flowering photos r17 and r18 in October and early November.

fruiting.note: Pods exceed 5 cm by late November and ripen in late December in northern Córdoba (Galera 2000); Wikipedia (es) reports November to March; iNaturalist fruiting histogram records December (3), January (4), February (1), April (1) and July (1), matching photos r19 (January) and r20 (February).

leaf_fall.note: Galera (2000) describes it as strictly deciduous, dropping leaves in winter when frosts arrive or as new growth breaks; photos r09 (June) and r10 (July) show thinning frost-dulled foliage and r11 (late August) shows bare branches.

leaf_tones.note: Bud break in September (Galera 2000); bright yellow-green new leaves in October photos r01, r06 and r15.
Full green to olive-green mature foliage from late spring through early winter (photos r16 in November, r05 in December, r12 in March, r03 in May and r09 in June).
Winter frosts dry and dull the remaining leaves before they drop (Galera 2000; photos r09 in June and r10 in July).

rainfall_mm_year.note: Occurs in Argentina from 300 to 1,200 mm/year, with greatest abundance between 500 and 800 mm/year (Adámoli 1973 in Galera 2000).

drought_tolerance.note: High resistance to aridity and drought, thriving down to 300 mm annual rainfall.

waterlogging_tolerance.note: Sources disagree: Giménez & Moglia (2003, citing López et al. 1995) report tolerance of poor drainage and prolonged flooding in palm-woodland depressions, whereas Galera (2000) states it does not thrive on heavy clay or saline soils.

shade_tolerance_seedling.note: Heliophilous species with low shade tolerance.

shade_tolerance_adult.note: Heliophilous species with low shade tolerance.

root_suckers.note: Resprouts readily from roots, especially under grazing or trampling.

resprouts.note: Vigorous coppice resprouting from stumps; juvenile trees resist fire.

density_kg_m3.note: Air-dry wood density: 830 kg/m³ at 15% moisture (CADAMDA), 850 kg/m³ (Giménez & Moglia 2003), and 900 kg/m³ dry or 1,170 kg/m³ green (INTI).

uses: sweet pod flour (patay), syrup (arrope) and drinks (añapa, aloja)
bark and wood tannins for leather
